misconceptions.statement: 1 is a prime number because it is divisible by 1 and itself.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the divisible-by-1-and-itself definition literally without noting it needs exactly two distinct factors.
misconceptions.fix: A prime has exactly two different factors. 1 has only one factor, so it is neither prime nor composite.

probe.question: Is 1 a prime number? Give a reason.
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 1 is divisible by 1 and by itself.

misconceptions.root_belief: a definition's surface wording is the whole definition
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student understanding of primes in number theory

misconceptions.statement: All odd numbers are prime and 2 is not prime because it is even.
misconceptions.why: Most primes seen are odd, so students link primeness with being odd.
misconceptions.fix: 2 is prime (only factors 1 and 2) and is the only even prime. Odd numbers like 9 and 15 are composite.
misconceptions.root_belief: a common example shows the general rule
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student concepts of prime numbers

misconceptions.statement: A factor tree can stop at any factor like 4 or 9 once the numbers look small.
misconceptions.why: Students stop splitting when numbers seem simple without checking for primality.
misconceptions.fix: Keep splitting until every branch end is a prime number.

probe.question: Write the prime factorisation of 36 using a factor tree: 36 = 4 × 9.

misconceptions.root_belief: a procedure ends when it looks done

misconceptions.statement: A number can have different prime factorisations, like 12 = 2×6 and 12 = 3×4.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse any factor pair with prime factorisation.
misconceptions.fix: Apart from order, prime factorisation is unique: 12 = 2×2×3 always.

probe.question: Is the prime factorisation of 12 unique?
probe.wrong_answer: No, 2×6 and 3×4 are both valid ones.

misconceptions.root_belief: two names for similar things are the same

misconceptions.statement: Writing the primes in a different order gives a different factorisation.
misconceptions.why: Students read the product as an ordered list like a numeral.
misconceptions.fix: Multiplication is commutative, so 2×3×5 and 5×3×2 are the same factorisation.

probe.question: Are 2×3×5 and 5×2×3 different prime factorisations of 30?

misconceptions.root_belief: order always changes meaning

misconceptions.why: Students read the exponent as multiplication by the base or as a repeat count.
misconceptions.fix: 2^3 = 2×2×2 = 8 and 3^2 = 9, so the product is 72.
misconceptions.root_belief: a power means multiply base by exponent
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student errors with exponents

misconceptions.statement: A number ending in 0 only needs 2 or 5 as a factor, not both.
misconceptions.why: Students notice that even numbers and multiples of 5 look related to ending digits.
misconceptions.fix: Ending in 0 means divisible by 10, so both 2 and 5 must appear in the prime factorisation.

probe.question: Can 6^n end in digit 0?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, since 6^n has factor 2, it can end in 0.

misconceptions.root_belief: one matching feature is enough to qualify

misconceptions.statement: To show 4^n or 6^n cannot end in 0, you must compute many values of n and check.
misconceptions.why: Students prefer testing examples over using the factorisation theorem.
misconceptions.fix: Use prime factorisation: 4^n = 2^(2n) has no factor 5, so it never ends in 0 for any n.

probe.question: Show that 4^n never ends in 0.
probe.wrong_answer: 4, 16, 64, 256 do not end in 0, so it never does.

misconceptions.root_belief: a few examples prove a general claim
misconceptions.source_hint: research on proof and empirical reasoning in school mathematics

misconceptions.statement: HCF is found by multiplying all the prime factors of both numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse HCF with LCM or product.
misconceptions.fix: HCF uses only primes common to both numbers, each with its smallest power.
misconceptions.root_belief: similar-sounding procedures are interchangeable
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' confusion between HCF and LCM

misconceptions.statement: For HCF take the greatest power of each common prime.
misconceptions.why: The word 'highest' suggests choosing the highest power.
misconceptions.fix: The highest common factor takes the smallest power of each common prime, since it must divide both numbers.
misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: If two numbers share no prime factors, they have no HCF.
misconceptions.why: Students think HCF must be a visible common factor greater than 1.
misconceptions.fix: 1 divides every number, so the HCF is 1 (the numbers are co-prime).
misconceptions.root_belief: nothing visible means nothing exists

misconceptions.statement: LCM takes only the common primes, using the smallest power.
misconceptions.why: Students carry the HCF rule over to LCM.
misconceptions.fix: LCM takes every prime that appears in either number, with its greatest power.
misconceptions.root_belief: one procedure fits similar problems
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on students' confusion between HCF and LCM

misconceptions.statement: LCM must be bigger than both numbers, so the LCM of 4 and 12 is 48.
misconceptions.why: Students think multiplying gives the 'common multiple' and that LCM must be larger than both.
misconceptions.fix: LCM can equal the larger number when it is a multiple of the other, so LCM of 4 and 12 is 12.
misconceptions.root_belief: combining always makes a bigger result

misconceptions.statement: HCF × LCM of two numbers equals their sum.
misconceptions.why: Students misremember which operation links them.
misconceptions.fix: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.

probe.question: If HCF(6,8)=2 and LCM=24, check the relation.

misconceptions.root_belief: remembered formulas are interchangeable

misconceptions.statement: HCF × LCM = product of numbers holds for three numbers too.
misconceptions.why: Students extend a two-number rule to any count.
misconceptions.fix: The rule is true only for two numbers; for three it generally fails.
misconceptions.root_belief: a rule for two works for any number

misconceptions.statement: Any long decimal with many digits is irrational.
misconceptions.why: Students judge irrationality by length rather than pattern.
misconceptions.fix: A decimal is irrational only if it neither terminates nor repeats; long terminating or repeating decimals are rational.

probe.question: Is 0.142857142857... rational?
probe.wrong_answer: Irrational, since it goes on forever.

misconceptions.root_belief: longer or more means a different kind
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' conceptions of rational and irrational numbers

misconceptions.statement: 22/7 is exactly π, so π is rational.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks and exams use 22/7 as a value for π.
misconceptions.fix: 22/7 is only an approximation; π is irrational with non-terminating non-repeating decimal expansion.
misconceptions.root_belief: an approximation is the exact value
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on pi and irrational numbers in school

misconceptions.statement: The square root of any number is irrational.
misconceptions.why: Students recall √2 and √3 as the standard examples.
misconceptions.fix: √n is rational when n is a perfect square, e.g. √16 = 4.

probe.question: Is √25 irrational?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a square root so irrational.

misconceptions.root_belief: a common example shows the general rule
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student concepts of irrational numbers

misconceptions.statement: A number like 0.5 or -3 cannot be rational since it is not written as a fraction.
misconceptions.why: Students see 'rational' as only meaning a visible p/q form.
misconceptions.fix: A number is rational if it can be written as p/q with q ≠ 0; 0.5 = 1/2 and -3 = -3/1.

probe.question: Is 0.5 a rational number?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a decimal, not a fraction.

misconceptions.root_belief: form shown determines the kind of number
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student concepts of rational numbers

misconceptions.statement: In the proof of √2 irrational, p and q can share factors, since we only need p²=2q².
misconceptions.why: Students skip the 'lowest terms' assumption as a technicality.
misconceptions.fix: We assume p/q is in lowest terms; showing both are even contradicts that.

probe.question: Why do we assume p and q are co-prime?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not needed; any p and q work.

misconceptions.root_belief: steps in a proof are just ritual
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student understanding of proof by contradiction

misconceptions.statement: A contradiction means our proof is wrong, so the original claim is false.
misconceptions.why: Students treat reaching a contradiction as a failed attempt.
misconceptions.fix: The contradiction shows that our assumption was false, so the opposite statement (irrational) is true.

probe.question: We assumed √2 is rational and got a contradiction. What does it show?
probe.wrong_answer: Our calculation is wrong; √2 is rational.

misconceptions.root_belief: reaching a contradiction means an error was made

misconceptions.statement: 3 + √2 is rational because 3 is rational.
misconceptions.why: Students think a rational part makes the whole rational.
misconceptions.fix: A rational plus an irrational is always irrational, so 3 + √2 is irrational.
misconceptions.root_belief: the whole takes the nature of one part

misconceptions.statement: The sum of two irrationals is always irrational.
misconceptions.why: Closure-style thinking is carried over from familiar number sets.
misconceptions.fix: Sums or products of irrationals can be rational: √2 + (−√2) = 0 and √2 × √2 = 2.

probe.question: Is √2 × √2 irrational?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, irrational times irrational is irrational.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule that works for most cases works always
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student reasoning about irrational number operations

misconceptions.statement: HCF is always larger than LCM since 'highest' beats 'lowest'.
misconceptions.why: Students rank the words 'highest' and 'lowest' rather than the numbers.
misconceptions.fix: HCF divides both numbers so it is at most the smaller number, while LCM is at least the larger number.

probe.question: Which is bigger, HCF or LCM of 6 and 8?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
